newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Barry Callebaut aims to compete with U.S. giants.
newsitem.headline: Barry Callebaut aims to compete with U.S. giants.

text.p: Barry Callebaut, formed from a merger of France's Cacao Barry SA and Swiss Callebaut AG, wants to compete with U.S. giants Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) and Cargill Inc in the cocoa and chocolate supplier market, its executives said.

"We wanted to represent a European alternative" to those firms, said Swiss investor Klaus Jacobs, chairman of Barry Callebaut. He was speaking at one of four separate European news briefings, ahead of an initial public offering (IPO) expected in January or February.
Barry Callebaut is a unit of Zurich-based Klaus J Jacobs Holding, but also has main offices near Paris, and in other countries including Belgium.

To smooth Belgian regulator approval for the merger, Barry Callebaut said it also agreed to sell Beldek, a Belgian firm held by its Cacao Goemaere unit. It said the sale would pave the way for Belgian regulatory approval of the merger deal.
Belgium's anti-trust authority said earlier it ruled against the planned merger because it would reinforce Callebaut's dominant position and hamper competition.
With respect to the U.K., a regulatory decision was still pending and would likely require time after the new U.K. Labour government took office following British elections May 1.

The merger of the Swiss and French companies, announced last July, created the world's largest cocoa bean grinding company, putting it ahead of ADM's and Cargill's cocoa grinding divisions, which are the world's second- and third-largest, respectively, Jacobs said.
The firm is also a major force in the finished chocolate and chocolate coatings market.

Jacobs said Barry Callebaut's main advantage versus its adversaries was its closeness to its customers, through its 19 separate production sites. Jacobs also said Barry Callebaut has "by far" the most extensive research and development departments among its competitors.
"When we merged, some people said we should get rid of some of the (R&D) people. I said no," Jacobs said.
The firm is looking to early 1998 as a likely date for its planned initial public offering (IPO), company executives said.
Jacobs also said the initial share sale was likely to entail less than 50 percent of Barry Callebaut.
Listing is expected in Switzerland. Paris and Brussels are also being considered for possible further listing.

Barry Callebaut reported revenues of 1.765 billion Swiss francs for its first business year to the end of August, and an operating profit of 111.7 million francs. After tax earnings for the first business year totaled 59.7 million francs.
The company gave no comparisons for the previous year.
It said business continued to develop well in the first half of the current year. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
